Antibiotic resistance genes in aquaculture: Molecular detection, environmental dynamics, and biological control strategies
Bridging soil resistome and clinical inference: A four-tier evidentiary framework
Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: proMGE2-a planetary-scale resource of mobile genetic elements in microbial (meta)genomes
abstract: proMGE is a resource of prokaryotic mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that systematically catalogues MGEs from prokaryotes, their intercellular spread, antimicrobial resistance gene carriage, and MGE nesting interactions. We present proMGE2 featuring a 6X expansion, a total of >16.4 million MGEs from 670k high-quality isolate genomes, and 180k metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), spanning diverse MGE categories: transposons and insertion sequences, phages, phage-like elements, conjugative elements, mobility islands, and integrons. proMGE2 includes MGEs from MAGs derived from environmental microbiomes, encompassing ~50k samples across several major habitat types. proMGE2 provides a standardized MGE reference collection of >5 million non-redundant MGE sequences drawn from our curated database, and enables identification of MGEs in user-provided genomes. proMGE2 captures MGE diversity and their functional potential at unprecedented scale to support future research of mobile genetic elements and transfer of genetic material in microbes. The database is available at http://promge.embl.de/.

title: Respiratory Infections at Mass Gatherings: A Travel-Medicine Review with Hajj and Umrah as a Longitudinal Case Study
abstract: Mass gatherings combine international mobility with dense, repeated contact and can amplify respiratory infections across travel corridors. Hajj, Umrah and Kumbh Mela, offer a uniquely recurrent case study, while other religious or sporting mega-events, and music or cultural festivals provide contrasting exposure systems. A focused narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and authoritative public-health guidance. Searches and project evidence synthesis prioritized publications from January 2021 to August 2026, with selected foundational sources. We examined respiratory symptoms, laboratory detections, clinical disease, vaccination, antimicrobial use and resistance, surveillance, environmental modifiers, and pre-, during-, and post-travel practice. No meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken. Respiratory risk is determined less by attendance alone than by contact intensity, duration, ventilation, vocalization, shared accommodation, traveler susceptibility, and pathogen circulation. Recent Hajj evidence confirms a substantial burden of respiratory symptoms and clinical consultations, but estimates vary because denominators range from volunteers and tested samples to healthcare encounters. Rhinovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and bacterial pneumonia remain important. There is continued abuse of antibiotics for predominantly viral syndromes and acquisition of resistant organisms link individual care to global antimicrobial resistance. Syndromic, laboratory, event-based, genomic, and wastewater surveillance are complementary, not interchangeable. Heat, dust, air quality, fatigue, and differential access to protective infrastructure modify respiratory symptoms, severity, and care seeking. Comparative events share mechanisms but not directly transferable rates. Travel-medicine practice should treat mass gatherings as longitudinal exposure systems spanning preparation, transport, the event, and return. Layered vaccination, risk-based masking, ventilation and crowd-flow measures, prompt diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and explicit travel histories, can reduce respiratory morbidity while preserving denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

title: The Interrelation between Phenotypic Properties and Sequence Type in Clinical Isolates of the Klebsiella Pneumoniae Species Complex
abstract: A comparative study of the biological properties (phenotypic characteristics and sequence types) of clinical isolates of Klebsiella pneumoniae obtained from two pediatric multidisciplinary hospitals (PMH-1 and PMH-2) was carried out. All isolates exhibited high levels of antimicrobial resistance (up to 100%), including resistance to third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, while over 70% remained susceptible to meropenem. Strains from PMH-2 demonstrated resistance to polyvalent Klebsiella bacteriophage (up to 75%) and a weak biofilm-forming capacity (84.4%). According to sequence typing data, strains with different genetic characteristics prevailed in each hospital: strains of the K2 serotype and different sequence types were detected mainly in PMH-1, whereas strains with the sequence type ST307 predominated in PMH-2. The biofilm-forming capacity, the K2 capsular type, and the presence of various sequence types determine population heterogeneity and contribute to increased drug resistance of these Klebsiella strains.

title: Chemical characterization, antibacterial activity, in vitro cytotoxicity, and selectivity of the lipid extract from Sargassum filipendula against multidrug-resistant bacteria
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria necessitates new therapeutic alternatives, and marine macroalgae represent an underexplored source of bioactive lipids. This study characterized the lipid extract (LE) of Sargassum filipendula and evaluated its antibacterial and cytotoxic profiles against MDR hospital isolates. LE composition was determined by GC-MS, and its thermal behavior by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Antibacterial activity was evaluated using the broth microdilution method (CLSI M07) against Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and coagulase-negative staphylococci, followed by determination of the minimum bactericidal concentration. Cytotoxicity was assessed in L929 and MDBK cell lines using MTT, Neutral Red, and Lactate Dehydrogenase assays; Hemolytic activity was evaluated using erythrocytes; and selectivity indices (SI) were calculated for each bacterial species. Palmitic acid (61.07%) and oleic acid (15.90%) were the predominant fatty acids. TGA revealed a total mass loss of 82% across two decomposition stages (296 °C, 445 °C), and DSC detected no phase transitions between - 80 and 270 °C. The LE exhibited bacteriostatic activity against all isolates, with MIC values ranging from 1.18 mg/mL (S. aureus) to 2.5 mg/mL (P. aeruginosa). Cytotoxicity assays yielded ICvalues ranging from 0.16 to 1.25 mg/mL, and the hemolytic ICwas 12.81 mg/mL. However, assay-specific SI values were ≤ 1.06 for adherent cells and 5.12-10.86 for erythrocytes. The S. filipendula LE is a candidate source of antibacterial compounds against MDR bacteria, although purification processes and in vivo validation are required to establish its therapeutic potential.

title: Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus: biological basis and prospects for antimicrobial application
abstract: The rapid rise of antimicrobial resistance has become a major global health challenge, particularly due to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria with complex resistance mechanisms and strong biofilm-forming capacity. Simultaneously, conventional antibiotic development has struggled to keep pace with the increasing prevalence of resistant pathogens, prompting renewed interest in alternative antimicrobial strategies. Among these, predatory bacteria, particularly Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus and related organisms collectively termed Bdellovibrio and like organisms (BALOs), have emerged as promising biologically driven agents capable of selectively targeting Gram-negative pathogens. This review examines the biology and predatory behaviour of B. bacteriovorus in the context of its proposed application as a "living antibiotic". The evolutionary background, taxonomy, cellular organisation, and biphasic life cycle of the organism are discussed to establish a framework for understanding its predatory efficiency. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular mechanisms involved in prey recognition, periplasmic invasion, intracellular growth, and the distinctive non-binary mode of cell division. Evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies evaluating activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections is critically assessed, together with current insights into host immune interactions and safety considerations. Recent advances in imaging technologies, genetic tools, and regulatory pathway analyses have substantially expanded the mechanistic understanding of Bdellovibrio biology. Beyond therapeutic applications, BALOs also demonstrate potential in agriculture, aquaculture, food safety, and environmental management. Although challenges related to large-scale production, delivery strategies, and regulatory acceptance remain, current evidence supports BALOs as promising components of future antimicrobial frameworks.

title: Host-Directed Ferroptotic Stress Modulation Against Intracellular Bacterial Infections: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Translational Challenges
abstract: The rise in antibiotic resistance and the persistence of intracellular infections underscore the urgent need for novel antimicrobial agents and strategies. Ferroptotic stress is a cell state marked by transiently elevated Felevels, increased lipid peroxidation, and altered redox balance. It has gained significant attention due to its role in the progression of various diseases, especially bacterial infections. By inducing intracellular iron overload, disrupting the bacterial microenvironment, and activating innate immune cells like macrophages, it serves as a crucial strategy to restrict intracellular bacterial growth and limit the emergence of resistance. Despite growing interest, systematic reviews integrating host ferroptotic stress modulation with precision antimicrobial strategies remain scarce. This review explores recent advancements in host-directed ferroptotic stress strategies for combating bacterial infections, focusing on metabolic reprogramming, macrophage-mediated defense, membrane remodeling, nutrient deprivation, iron trafficking, direct bacteriolysis, and antibiotic synergism. It highlights the potential of precision modulation of host ferroptotic stress to enhance antimicrobial strategies and identifies key research gaps to advance related therapeutic approaches.

title: Bacteria-Induced Outer Membrane Disruption and Sensitization by Rationally Designed Proamyloid Peptides
abstract: In the era of increasing antimicrobial resistance and diminishing antibiotic pipeline, the use of antibiotic adjuvants that decrease the excessive use of antibiotics while preserving the efficacy holds considerable promise. In this study, we report the design of cationic 23-residue proamyloidogenic peptides with no antimicrobial properties that can sensitize Gram-negative bacteria to antibiotics. In experimental model, peptides-antibiotic (half-dose) combination significantly decreases the bacterial burden and disease severity in comparison to monotherapies. We show that the peptides agglutinate bacteria cells and form amyloid fibrils by interacting with the outer membrane components, facilitating the antibiotic uptake. The peptides self-assemble only in the presence of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and do not form similar structures in the presence of negatively charged liposomes/micelles. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) are used to study the peptides-lipopolysaccharide complex structure. The proposed approach offers a promising strategy that can potentiate the antibiotic activity of existing antibiotics and minimize excessive use of antibiotics, expanding the antibiotic armamentarium.

title: The σ subunit identity, rather than RbpA, is the major determinant of M. tuberculosis RNA polymerase sensitivity to fidaxomicin
abstract: Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) at an early stage of transcription initiation. Fidaxomicin is used for treating Clostridioides difficile infections and has demonstrated in vitro efficacy against drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Fidaxomicin derivatives are currently the focus of extensive research to develop novel antibacterial agents. Previous studies showed that region 3.2 of the RNAP primary σ factor and the mycobacterial transcriptional activator RbpA modulate fidaxomicin potency through poorly understood mechanisms. Moreover, the impact of the structurally distinct extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors on fidaxomicin potency has never been explored. Here, using DNA scaffold-based in vitro transcription assays, we found that RbpA-dependent primary σ factors from Mtb enhance fidaxomicin potency, whereas ECF σ factors render Mtb RNAP resistant to fidaxomicin. Contrary to the prevailing assumptions, RbpA has only a marginal effect on fidaxomicin potency. Our structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations support a model in which ECF σ factors obstruct fidaxomicin binding by changing the configuration of the RNAP RNA channel. Conversely, the direct interaction between fidaxomicin and RbpA-dependent primary σ factors does not affect drug binding. Our findings identify the σ factor as a key modulator of fidaxomicin potency and provide a framework to explore σ factor structural diversity for designing pathogen-specific fidaxomicin analogs. Moreover, these results highlight fundamental mechanistic differences between the modes of action of housekeeping and ECF σ factors during transcription initiation.

title: Closely related Vibrio alginolyticus and Vibrio diabolicus share largely similar phenotypic and genetic virulence traits
abstract: Vibrio alginolyticus is associated with opportunistic wound and ear infections, whereas the human pathogenic potential of the closely related species Vibrio diabolicus remains unclear. In this study, 29 Vibrio strains initially identified as V. alginolyticus were investigated, including 21 clinical and eight environmental isolates. Species identification was reassessed using average nucleotide identity (OrthoANI) based on whole-genome sequencing. In addition, 45 virulence-associated genes were screened, and biofilm formation, motility, hemolysis, human serum resistance, and antimicrobial susceptibility were characterized. Genome-based taxonomic analysis reassigned eight strains, including five clinical isolates, to V. diabolicus. The majority of investigated virulence-associated genes were universally present across the strain collection, including genes related to adhesion, quorum sensing, chemotaxis, iron acquisition, secretion systems, flagellar function, and stress response. Only a limited number of markers showed variable distribution: tlh was detected in 28/29 strains, whereas tdh, trh, ctxAB, and rtx were absent, and VPI-associated genes were detected in one strain. Phenotypic distributions largely overlapped between species. β-Hemolysis on human blood agar occurred in 83% of strains, and 97% were resistant to ampicillin. Biofilm formation was generally stronger at 25 °C, whereas swimming migration zone diameters were generally larger at 37 °C and after 48 h than after 24 h. Clinical isolates tended to show higher human serum resistance than environmental isolates. Overall, the investigated V. alginolyticus and V. diabolicus strains showed substantial overlap in phenotypic traits and the investigated virulence-associated genes, indicating that individual virulence-associated markers alone are insufficient to reliably assess human pathogenic potential.

title: DNA uptake and twitching motility are controlled by small RNA Arp through repression of pilin translation in Acinetobacter baumannii
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a major opportunistic pathogen capable of natural transformation. This process is driven by type IV pili (T4P) facilitating horizontal gene transfer and accelerating the spread of antimicrobial resistance. While the transcriptional regulation of T4P is increasingly understood, post-transcriptional mechanisms controlling pilus assembly remain unexplored. Here, we identify and mechanistically characterise a small RNA, Arp (Acinetobacter repressor of pilin), as a post-transcriptional repressor of T4P-mediated functions in A. baumannii. Previous proximity RNA-RNA ligation experiments using High throughput Global sRNA target Identification by Ligation and Sequencing (Hi-GRIL-seq), indicated interactions between Arp and the 5' end of the pilA mRNA, encoding the major pilin subunit PilA. Here, in-line probing and translational reporter assays revealed that Arp represses pilA translation in A. baumannii by sequestering the Shine-Dalgarno sequence and the first seven codons of the pilA mRNA. Accordingly, deletion of arp increases DNA uptake and twitching motility, while overexpression of Arp depletes pilA mRNA from A. baumannii cells significantly impairing DNA uptake and twitching motility-two hallmark T4P-dependent phenotypes. Together, our study identifies a native A. baumannii sRNA that modulates natural competence by targeting pilin synthesis, revealing a new regulatory layer that could be exploited to disrupt horizontal gene transfer in multidrug-resistant strains.

title: Analysis of antimicrobial resistance in the LAKANA trial of azithromycin administration in Mali: A sub-study of a cluster randomized clinical trial
abstract: Mass azithromycin administration has been used to reduce under-five mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, but concerns remain about its potential impact on antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The Large-scale Assessment of the Key health-promoting Activities of two New mass drug administration regiments with Azithromycin (LAKANA) trial was a cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Mali, enrolling infants aged 1-11 months randomized to placebo, twice-yearly azithromycin, or quarterly azithromycin for 2 years. The trial did not find any mortality benefit amongst treated children. The current analysis is a sub-study of the parent trial examining AMR outcomes. Repeated cross-sectional nasopharyngeal and rectal swabs were collected from children aged 4-14-months in villages randomized to placebo, twice-yearly or quarterly azithromycin, and from untreated contacts aged 49-59-months at baseline, 12-, 24-, and 36-months post-village enrollment across 59 LAKANA trial villages. Phenotypic resistance to macrolide and nonmacrolide antibiotics was assessed in Streptococcus pneumoniae (S. pneumoniae) and Escherichia coli (E. coli) isolates using disk diffusion or E-tests. The primary noninferiority analysis evaluated macrolide resistance prevalence at 36-months among younger children and at 24-months among older contacts, with predefined margin of +10 percentage points. A total of 5,025 nasopharyngeal and 5,021 rectal samples were analyzed. At baseline, among 4-14-month-old children, macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae was 16.6%, 15.5%, and 11.1% in the placebo, twice-yearly and quarterly azithromycin groups, respectively, and 5.0%, 5.0%, and 0.0% in E. coli. At 36-months, corresponding prevalences were 13.4%, 14.5%, and 17.2% for S. pneumoniae, and 5.1%, 6.4%, and 9.1% for E. coli. The difference between placebo and twice-yearly groups was 1.0% (95% CI [-4.7, 6.8]) for S. pneumoniae and 1.3% (95% CI [-2.4, 4.9]) for E. coli; corresponding differences for quarterly azithromycin group was 3.8% (95% CI [-3.3, 10.9]) for S. pneumoniae and 4.0% (95% CI [-0.7, 8.7]) for E. coli. Among untreated older children, there were no marked inter-group differences in macrolide resistance either at baseline or at 24-months. The study may not have been large enough to detect a small increase in macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae among young children in villages that received quarterly azithromycin. Twice-yearly azithromycin administration to 1-11-month-old infants for 2 years in Mali did not increase macrolide resistance in treated children or untreated contacts and met the predefined noninferiority margin in tested isolates. Quarterly administration, however, cannot exclude a modest dose-dependent increase of macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae and E. coli.

title: Bloodstream Infection Pathogen Profiles in ICU and Non-ICU Patients in a Tertiary Hospital in Southern Anhui, China
abstract: Bloodstream infection (BSI) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. We retrospectively analyzed 723 adults with blood culture-confirmed BSI from January 2025 to March 2026, including 253 ICU and 470 non-ICU patients, and compared clinical characteristics, infection sources, invasive procedures, pathogen distribution, antimicrobial use, resistance phenotypes, and antimicrobial susceptibility. ICU patients had higher rates of septic shock and in-hospital mortality and more frequent catheter-related and lower respiratory tract infections and invasive procedures. Gram-negative bacteria predominated in both groups, with Escherichia coli ranking first. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Enterococcus spp. accounted for larger proportions in ICU patients. Special-use antimicrobial use, particularly carbapenem use, was higher in the ICU. Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were significantly more frequent in ICU patients, whose major Gram-negative isolates also showed broader resistance profiles. These findings support care-setting-specific pathogen and resistance surveillance to inform empirical antimicrobial therapy, antimicrobial stewardship, and infection-control strategies.

title: Engineering mRNA-Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against multidrug resistant bacteria: current and future prospects
abstract: This review highlights the significant potential of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology for application in bacterial vaccines, with a long-term goal to provide critical tools in controlling problematic microbial infections regardless of their antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profile. The current landscape of bacterial vaccine development, including methods for identification of candidate antigens, are discussed along with emerging design principles for LNP delivery systems. We focus on mRNA-LNP systems for delivery of bacterial vaccine antigens in large part due to their extensive clinical validation, compatibility with reverse vaccinology, and growing prominence in modern vaccinology. Attention is also given to emerging opportunities to develop effective tools to combat severe infections, particularly those caused by AMR bacterial infections. Specific advantages and challenges of RNA-based vaccine platforms and LNP delivery systems compared to other vaccine modalities including strategies are highlighted, with a focus on particular strengths in conserved antigen identification via genome sequencing and recent advances in optimizing LNP composition for induction of strongly protective immunity for vaccine delivery. We argue that mRNA-LNP technology combined with reverse vaccinology approaches has the potential to improve and accelerate bacterial vaccine development, particularly for broadly protective immunity less dependent on bacterial strain surface composition and which are entirely dependent on host immunity, making them agnostic to the issue of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Antimicrobial and cytotoxic activities of Ag/AgCl nanoparticles biosynthesized by Bacillus cereus against multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa from hospital environments
abstract: Hospital surfaces can serve as reservoirs for multidrug resistant (MDR) Pseudomonas aeruginosa․ Continuous and effective surface-directed decontamination strategies are required․ The current study investigates the use of Bacillus cereus-biosynthesized Ag/AgCl nanoparticles as an antimicrobial surface-directed decontamination strategy for drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolated from hospital samples․ An environmental screening of three hospitals found P. aeruginosa in 23 of 224 environmental swabs (10․3%), with sinks being the most contaminated sampling location (39.1% of positive samples)․ Phenotypic profiling revealed a concerning resistance spectrum: 26.1% MDR, 13% XDR, and 4.3% PDR, including a 13.0% incidence of colistin resistance. This is the first time that Ag/AgCl NPs have been biogenic produced from Bacillus cereus biomass' incorporating hospital environmental surveillance and the antimicrobial resistance profile with Ag/AgCl NPs biosynthesis and functional characterization toward MDR' XDR' and PDR local P. aeruginosa isolates' as well as the antibacterial and antibiofilm activity assessment of the synthesized Ag/AgCl NPs․ Comprehensive physicochemical characterization (UV-Vis, FTIR, XRD, TEM, FESEM, and zeta potential) confirmed the production of quasi-spherical, face-centered cubic (FCC) Ag/AgCl nanoparticles with a mean crystallite size of 9.58 nm and a zeta potential of - 30.7 mV, indicating moderate to good colloidal stability. The NPs demonstrated robust antibacterial activity, with a MIC of 24 µg/mL against all six tested P. aeruginosa strains, and achieved near-complete biofilm inhibition at concentrations ≥ 24 µg/mL. The Ag/AgCl nanoparticles had cytotoxicity in HaCaT keratinocytes lower than MIC concentration (IC = 13.8 µg/mL; SI = 0․575)' and the excessive cytotoxicity against normal cells may limit their clinical usage․ Nevertheless' additional studies may be required to pursue the use of unmodified Ag/AgCl nanoparticles as antimicrobial agents on vertical and horizontal surfaces in hospitals to eliminate drug-resistant P. aeruginosa from inanimate reservoirs․ Studies to optimize and standardize surface-disinfection methodologies will help determine the practical and safety implications of these systems․ These findings support the potential application of the biosynthesized Ag/AgCl nanoparticles in environmental surface decontamination; however, their effectiveness and safety on hospital surfaces require validation in standardized surface-based and simulated environmental models.

title: Genome-scale mining and experimental characterization of antimicrobial peptides from Bacillus
abstract: The escalating global crisis of antibiotic resistance necessitates the development of novel antibacterial agents. The genus Bacillus, a prolific producer of bioactive secondary metabolites, represents an important resource for the discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). In this study, we integrated large-scale genomic analysis with machine learning to systematically mine 3,283 high-quality Bacillus genomes from the NCBI database. A total of 6,532 putative AMP sequences were identified and clustered into 682 antimicrobial peptide cluster families (ACFs). Physicochemical analysis showed that Bacillus-derived AMPs are enriched in lysine, leucine, and isoleucine but depleted in cysteine. Despite their high sequence novelty and divergence from human- and animal-derived AMPs, these peptides exhibit similar biophysical characteristics, including net charge and hydrophobicity. APEX-based MIC predictions were used to prioritize a pool of 73 high-potency candidates, from which four peptides were selected for chemical synthesis and experimental validation. These peptides displayed species-dependent antibacterial activity, with the strongest activity observed against Clostridium perfringens. Experimental validation revealed species-dependent correlations, with strong positive correlations for three bacterial species (r = 0.967-0.970) but negative correlations for A. baumannii (r = - 0.557) and Salmonella Typhimurium (r = - 0.619). Steered molecular dynamics simulations indicated that AMP_3 and AMP_4 exhibited distinct membrane-translocation behaviors under the SMD pulling conditions, whereas AMP_2 showed stronger dependence on membrane surface charge. Overall, this study highlights the untapped biosynthetic potential of AMPs within Bacillus genomes and demonstrates that combining genomic mining with deep learning prediction is an effective strategy for accelerating the discovery of novel antibiotics.

title: Cell-based immunotherapies for infectious diseases: current evidence and translational perspectives on cytokine induced killer (CIK) cells
abstract: The persistent global burden of infectious diseases, compounded by environmental challenges, emerging pathogens, and antimicrobial resistance, underscores the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antimicrobial agents. Cell based immunotherapies, which harness the body's immune system to combat pathogens, have gained increasing attention for their potential to provide targeted, durable, and adaptive responses. Recently, we demonstrated that clinically licensed cytokine-induced killer (CIK) cells, used in cancer treatment, significantly reduced Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes in vitro. This review focuses on the emerging role of CIK cells in infectious disease therapy, positioning them alongside other prominent immune effector cells such as CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells. We explore the biology, recognition mechanisms, their potential feature, and cytotoxic functions of these cell populations, distinguishing direct findings in infection-specific CIK studies from mechanisms characterized in oncology or other cytotoxic lymphocytes. While CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells have been extensively studied for their roles in early and adaptive immune responses, CIK cells traditionally investigated in oncology, are now being recognized for their potential in antiviral and antimicrobial immunity. Alongside with CTLs, γδT cells, and NK cells, we detail CIK cell phenotypes, activation strategies, effector functions, and the limited but growing body of evidence supporting their application in some viral infections. The available findings support further investigation of CIK cells as a candidate approach in selected infectious settings, while their broader antimicrobial applicability, comparative efficacy, target specificity, safety, and clinical benefit require further evaluation in these settings.

title: Carbon availability in Staphylococcus aureus infection: cellular access, metabolic fate and antibiotic response
abstract: Carbon availability during Staphylococcus aureus infection is often equated with extracellular substrate concentration, although this measurement reveals neither cellular partitioning nor the intracellular fate of acquired carbon. This distinction becomes treatment-relevant because conditions that permit bacterial survival need not be those that later favor population recovery or resistant genotypes. Here, we synthesize infection-relevant evidence across five inferential levels: local substrate pool, cellular access, intracellular carbon fate, physiological state and antibiotic response. Applying this separation across time distinguishes immediate metabolic effects on killing from subsequent population recovery and resistant-variant expansion. In a diabetic skin-infection model, hyperglycaemia increased recovery of heritable rifampicin resistance without genomic evidence of hypermutability, consistent with altered population opportunity rather than a direct carbon-to-mutation mechanism. Across the evidence reviewed, no study in S. aureus has linked the measured carbon fate of a bacterium surviving antibiotic exposure to the recovery and resistance phenotypes of its descendants. We therefore propose a two-stage, non-obligatory model in which restrictive carbon conditions can modify survival during treatment, whereas restoration or rerouting of metabolically usable carbon can restore killing, permit susceptible regrowth or favor expansion of resistant variants. The model yields a lineage-specific, falsifiable prediction: carbon-restricted survivors contribute disproportionately to the recovered population and, under continued selection, to its resistant fraction. Testing this prediction requires experiments that preserve substrate identity, cellular identity, intracellular carbon fate and ancestry through recovery. By defining this unconnected causal step, the framework makes cellular descent testable and provides a basis for evaluating metabolic interventions across antibiotic-niche combinations.

title: Cobalt(III) Schiff Base Complexes as Irreversible Inhibitors of the Metallo-β-Lactamase NDM-1
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a critical public health concern, with approximately 2.8 million Americans infected with antibiotic-resistant bacteria annually and over 35,000 deaths in the United States alone. Of particular concern are Enterobacterales that express metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), bacteria that cause nosocomial infections and exhibit resistance to most β-lactam drugs. The zinc-containing active sites of MBLs differ from those of serine β-lactamases, making current clinical inhibitors ineffective. No FDA-approved MBL inhibitors exist, leaving a critical gap in therapeutics for MBL-expressing Enterobacterales infections. Herein, we biochemically and spectroscopically demonstrate irreversible inhibition of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 by a subset of cobalt(III) Schiff base complexes (Co(III)-sb). Crystallography and 59Co NMR experiments show that inactivation efficiency is dependent on axial and equatorial ligand identity. While Co(III)-sb exhibits NDM-1 inhibition, chemical modification is required to enable complexes to cross the Gram-negative envelope. These findings establish Co(III)-sb complexes as a novel scaffold for the development of MBL inhibitors.

title: Structural Basis of Self-Promoted Uptake of Cationic Antimicrobial Peptides across the Lipopolysaccharide-Rich Outer Membrane of Gram-Negative Bacteria
abstract: Lipopolysaccharide, a specialized multiacylated glycolipid, constitutes the outer leaflet of the outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria. Densely packed anionic LPS molecules, stabilized by divalent cations such as Mg2+ and Ca2+, form a formidable permeability barrier that restricts the entry of diverse molecules, including antibiotics, antibacterial proteins, and toxins. Pioneering studies from Bob Hancock's laboratory demonstrated that treatment of Gram-negative bacteria with polycationic antibiotics markedly enhances OM permeability to large proteins and hydrophobic compounds. This discovery led to the concept of self-promoted uptake pathway, a mechanism by which cationic antimicrobial agents gain access to bacterial cells through their own disruption of the LPS barrier. Cationic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), also known as host-defense peptides, exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and have emerged as promising candidates for combating the global crisis of antibiotic resistance. A critical component of their antibacterial mechanism is the permeabilization of the LPS-rich outer membrane through the self-promoted uptake pathway. This process involves a series of coordinated molecular events, including initial electrostatic recognition of LPS, peptide-induced structural reorganization of the outer membrane, perturbation of LPS acyl-chain packing, membrane-assisted peptide folding and oligomerization, and dynamic AMP-LPS interactions that collectively facilitate peptide translocation across the outer membrane. To commemorate Bob Hancock's seminal contributions to this field, we review recent advances in understanding AMP-mediated self-promoted uptake by integrating insights from atomic-resolution structural studies by NMR, biophysical investigations of AMP-LPS interactions, and molecular simulations of AMP-LPS membrane systems. Together, these studies provide a comprehensive structural framework for understanding how cationic AMPs overcome the LPS permeability barrier and permeabilize the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.

title: Synthesis of Aspergillomarasmine A and Toxin A Hydroxamic Acid Derivatives for Evaluation as Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitors
abstract: Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in Gram-negative bacteria is identified by the World Health Organization as a major threat to global health. Such resistance is increasingly mediated by serine- and metallo-β-lactamases, that catalyze beta-lactam hydrolysis. While serine-β-lactamase inhibitors are widely used in combination therapies, there is a lack of clinically approved metallo-β-lactamase inhibitors, although several promising candidates have been identified. Among these, the fungal natural product aspergillomarasmine A (AMA) inhibits metallo-β-lactamases including New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 (NDM-1), restoring the activity of meropenem against resistant isolates. Here, we report robust and scalable routes for the synthesis of AMA and toxin A, enabling selective modifications to be made at each carboxylic acid of the AMA scaffold. Seven hydroxamic acid derivatives were synthesized in addition to cyclic derivatives of AMA and toxin A. The inhibition activities (pIC50 values) of the compounds were evaluated against a range of isolated clinically relevant metallo-β-lactamases, including in the presence of different Zn(II) concentrations. Microbiological assays were performed, with AMA, toxin A, and their hydroxamic acid derivatives restoring the activity of meropenem against carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii strains, obtained from clinical and environmental isolates from Tanzania and Malawi, containing NDM-1 or NDM-5. The synthetic procedures and metallo-β-lactamase inhibition results described will promote and enable further optimization of metallo-β-lactamase inhibitors based on the AMA scaffold.

title: Targeting Force-Regulated FimH Adhesin: Assays, Mannosides, and Biologics for Anti-Virulence Therapy of UPEC Infection
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections, and recurrent UTIs caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) drive antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance. FimH, the mannose-binding adhesin at the tip of type 1 pili, is a central UPEC virulence factor. Under shear force, FimH switches from a low-affinity, tense state to a high-affinity, relaxed state, strengthening adhesion during urine flow. This catch-bond behavior makes FimH a promising anti-virulence target, though a difficult one to drug. Here, we review strategies to target FimH, including monovalent and multivalent mannosides, vaccines, conformation-selective monoclonal antibodies, and de novo engineered miniproteins, together with the assays used to quantify FimH-ligand binding and UPEC adhesion. Clinical translation has been limited by assay-dependent potency, urinary pharmacokinetics, and intracellular reservoirs. We posit that effective FimH-targeted therapy requires alignment among inhibitor mechanism, FimH conformational state, bladder lumen exposure, and infection stage, which in turn defines realistic roles in prevention, early intervention, and combination therapy.

title: Accumulation of Polyphosphate Inhibits Biofilm Formation in Mycobacteria by Activating RegX3 to Reduce Intracellular c-di-GMP Levels
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis can persist in the host for prolonged periods. Biofilm formation represents a key strategy that promotes bacterial persistence, enhances antibiotic resistance, and facilitates immune evasion. Thus, targeting biofilm formation holds significant therapeutic potential for tuberculosis. Exopolyphosphatase 1 (PPX1), highly conserved among mycobacteria, hydrolyzes inorganic polyphosphate. Although changes in polyphosphate levels are known to influence mycobacterial biofilm formation, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, using a Mycobacterium smegmatis model strain, we found that the level of polyphosphate in the Δppx1 mutant significantly increases, concomitant with impaired biofilm formation. Further investigation revealed that elevated polyphosphate enhances the transcriptional activity of the transcription factor RegX3, which in turn represses biofilm formation. Mechanistically, activated RegX3 directly binds to and upregulates the dcpA gene, encoding a bifunctional enzyme that lowers intracellular cyclic di-GMP levels. This reduction ultimately perturbs cell wall lipid synthesis and compromises biofilm formation. In summary, this work reveals a signaling pathway through which polyphosphate governs biofilm formation in M. smegmatis.

title: Predominance of viral core functions over auxiliary metabolism among carbohydrate-active enzymes annotated in the global soil virosphere
abstract: Soil viruses are increasingly recognized as components of microbial communities with the potential to alter ecosystem functioning, yet the frequency and functional distribution of virus-encoded metabolic genes in soils remain poorly understood. Here, the Global Soil Virus Atlas gene catalog, comprising 1,432,147 viral genes from 1,223 samples across 12 ecosystem types, was searched against KEGG, Pfam, and CAZy for functions related to carbon cycling, nitrogen cycling, and antimicrobial resistance. Annotations associated with host entry or cell-wall lysis were separated from putative auxiliary metabolic functions. Of 5,020 initial gene-level functional annotations across the three categories, 3,322 (66.2%) were classified as peptidoglycanases. Their exclusion left 1,698 genes (0.14% of the gene catalog restricted to contigs ≥10 kb), and carbon-cycling functions represented 96.7% of the enzyme-resolved annotations. Chitinase-associated genes formed the largest carbon category, but 78.0% belonged to GH19, a family containing both chitinases and phage endolysins. Among GH19 genes on contigs encoding detectable holins or spanins, 84.2% occurred within three genes of these lysis components, a distribution comparable to that of canonical phage lysozymes. Across six matched metagenomic studies, estimated viral contributions to the targeted functions ranged from 0.00% to 8.45% (mean: 2.27%). Two of the three estimates exceeding 2% were GH19-associated chitinase estimates from rhizosphere soils and were therefore treated as upper estimates. Thus, the putative soil viral metabolic inventory was sparse and concentrated in carbon-degradation functions, whereas much of the initial carbohydrate-active enzyme signal reflected core viral lysis functions rather than auxiliary metabolism. Soil microorganisms drive decomposition and nutrient cycling, and the viruses that infect them may alter these processes by carrying genes that affect host metabolism. However, genes annotated as carbohydrate-degradation enzymes may instead help viruses enter cells or break host cell walls when new virus particles are released. In a worldwide catalog of soil viruses, approximately two-thirds of the initial functional assignments represented these infection or release activities. After their removal, putative viral auxiliary metabolic genes were uncommon and concentrated mainly in carbon degradation. Genes potentially involved in chitin degradation were most frequent, but many occurred near viral genes used to break host cells; their estimated contribution should therefore be viewed as an upper limit. Distinguishing core viral functions from host metabolic modification is essential to avoid overestimating viral contributions to soil processes and to identify the strongest candidates for experimental testing.

title: Draft genome sequence of Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Emek SBI_BS17_EJ_BD isolate from Dhaka, Bangladesh
