title: Helicobacter pylori eradication and gastric cancer prevention: current evidence and future perspectives
abstract: infection is recognized as the principal etiological factor in gastric carcinogenesis, and despite the widespread implementation oferadication strategies, the global burden of gastric cancer remains substantial. This review summarizes the role of(through key bacterial survival mechanisms, epithelial colonization, immune evasion, and virulence factors that promote persistent inflammation and mucosal injury) in gastric carcinogenesis, focusing on the sequential gastric mucosal alterations described in the Correa cascade that are accompanied by activation of oncogenic signaling pathways. Relevant literature was identified from databases (including PubMed and Scopus). Recent translational studies have highlighted the complexity of-related determinants of GC progression, including bacterial virulence factors, alterations in the gastric environment, gastric microbiota, and host genetic susceptibility. However, the precise mechanisms underlying each determinant are still being elucidated. Therefore, in recent clinical practice, the early detection and eradication strategies remain the most realistic and impactful interventions. In the future, eradication-focused management may shift to a more stratified model that includes earlier screening in high-risk populations, wider use of susceptibility-guided or region-adapted therapy, and molecular risk surveillance after eradication, refining recent practice.

title: Visible-light degradation of ciprofloxacin by hierarchical Ag(3)PO(4)/CuInS(2) heterostructures: interfacial charge transfer, transformation pathways, and ecological risk context
abstract: Ciprofloxacin persists in aquatic environments and may contribute to antimicrobial resistance, creating demand for efficient, low-energy treatment technologies. In this study, a hierarchical flower-like AgPO/CuInSheterostructure was synthesized through a combined solvothermal-hydrothermal route and evaluated for visible-light-driven ciprofloxacin degradation. XRD, FTIR, Raman, XPS and elemental mapping confirmed the coexistence and interfacial coupling of cubic AgPOand chalcopyrite CuInS. The heterostructure consisted of faceted AgPOparticles integrated with flower-like CuInSaggregates and exhibited a surface area of 39.22 mg, average pore diameter of 47.70 nm and band gap of 1.92 eV. Photoluminescence quenching and a reduced impedance arc indicated improved interfacial charge migration and suppressed electron-hole recombination. Under visible light, the composite achieved 96.13% ciprofloxacin degradation within 60 min, compared with 44.30% for AgPOand 58.87% for CuInS, with a rate constant of 0.03561 min, 5.3 and 3.76 times higher, respectively. Maximum degradation occurred near pH 6.6, while excessive catalyst loading and higher ciprofloxacin concentration reduced efficiency. Radical-quenching experiments showed that photogenerated holes and hydroxyl radicals were the dominant oxidative species, with superoxide making a secondary contribution. A direct Z-scheme-like pathway was proposed, retaining strongly oxidizing holes in the AgPOvalence band and reducing electrons in the CuInSconduction band. LC-MS indicated piperazine oxidation,-dealkylation, ring opening, defluorination, decarboxylation and quinolone-ring cleavage. The heterostructure retained 89.45% degradation efficiency after four cycles, indicating promising reusability. These findings demonstrate enhanced charge separation, rapid antibiotic transformation, improved photocatalytic performance and promising visible-light treatment potential of antibiotic-contaminated water.

title: A dual-barrier sustained-release hydrogel based on Cu-exchanged Y zeolite and sodium alginate for infected wound healing
abstract: Bacterial wound infection and the growing crisis of antibiotic resistance urgently demand non-antibiotic wound dressings that integrate long-term antibacterial activity and high biosafety. Herein, we designed a dual-barrier sustained-release antibacterial hydrogel (CuY@SA) by embedding Cu-exchanged Y zeolite (CuY) into a calcium-crosslinked sodium alginate (SA) matrix. The ordered microporous zeolite acts as the first-stage reservoir to enable intrinsic Cusustained releaseion exchange, while the alginate network serves as a second physical diffusion barrier to suppress burst release and prolong delivery. The resulting CuY@SA hydrogel eliminated the initial burst and achieved nearly-linear Curelease over 48 h, with an equilibrium swelling ratio of approximately 28 g gin pH 7.4 PBS., CuY@SA exhibited over 99.9% bactericidal efficacy againstand, while maintaining >98% cytocompatibility with NIH-3T3 fibroblasts at hydrogel concentrations up to 10 mg mL. In a mouse full-thickness infected wound model, CuY@SA significantly accelerated wound closure to over 98% by day 14, promoted collagen deposition and re-epithelialization, reduced local inflammation, and caused no obvious organ toxicity or cuproptosis. Compared with the control hydrogel (Cu@SA) containing directly added free Cu, CuY@SA showed remarkably lower cytotoxicity and superiorantibacterial activity, confirming the critical role of zeolite in precise controlled release. This work demonstrates that combining an inorganic zeolite carrier with a biopolymer hydrogel provides a simple, scalable, and effective strategy for developing safe and long-acting antibacterial wound dressings. More broadly, it highlights the untapped potential of zeolites as versatile and tunable controlled-release platforms for advanced biomedical applications.

title: Genetic diversity and resistance profiles of MRSA in community and healthcare settings
abstract: This study aimed to characterize and compare methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains isolated from community members and healthcare workers (HCWs) in Egypt using antibiotic susceptibility testing, mecA gene detection, SCCmec typing, and ERIC-PCR fingerprinting. A cross-sectional study was conducted between September 2024 and January 2025, during which 450 specimens were collected from Mansoura University Hospitals and the local community, where 71 specimens (30.8%) were confirmed as MRSA. MRSA prevalence was significantly higher among HCWs, 62.5% (50/80), than among community members, 14% (21/150). In general, antibiotic resistance rates were higher in HCW strains. All isolates were resistant to cefoxitin and sensitive to vancomycin.The methicillin-resistant phenotype of the 71 MRSA isolates was confirmed by positive mecA gene tests, with SCCmec Type III prevalent among healthcare workers and SCCmec Type IV predominating in the community. ERIC-PCR fingerprinting demonstrated the isolates' genetic diversity. The dendrogram based on ERIC patterns showed distinct clusters between community and hospital strains, though with some overlap, suggesting possible transmission between the two populations.In conclusion, MRSA strains from HCWs displayed broader antibiotic resistance and greater clonal similarity, while community strains were more diverse and less resistant. The presence of intermixed clusters between community-acquired (CA-MRSA) and (HCW-MRSA) suggested a possible bidirectional transmission pathway, underscoring the blurring of epidemiological boundaries.These results underline the necessity of ongoing molecular surveillance and integrated infection control strategies to track the spread of MRSA in community and clinical settings.

title: Discovery and development of antimicrobial polymers
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is among the most pressing healthcare challenges of our time. Multidrug-resistant 'superbugs' continue to emerge at an alarming rate, while antibiotic development has stalled in recent decades. Antimicrobial peptides have attracted interest for their potent bactericidal activity and lower propensity to spur resistance; however, translation into clinical practice has been hampered by poor bioavailability, challenging syntheses and limited stability. By contrast, synthetic copolymers mimicking antimicrobial peptides have received attention for their efficacy and synthetic tractability. Here we highlight recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discuss future directions for their design and implementation. We also outline future research directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods that ensure the worldwide accessibility of these materials.

title: Neonatal sepsis
abstract: Neonatal sepsis and preterm birth are leading contributors to childhood death and disability in sepsis survivors. Whereas deaths from infectious diseases of childhood have declined substantially worldwide, progress in reducing neonatal sepsis burden and impact has stagnated in many low-income and middle-income countries. Efforts to track and prevent neonatal sepsis are hampered by the lack of a universally accepted case definition, gaps in global surveillance programmes, varied clinical presentations, and paucity of accurate and affordable sepsis diagnostics. The changing epidemiology of neonatal sepsis with predominance of Gram-negative pathogens, antimicrobial resistance, scarcity of and inequitable access to novel antibiotics, and under-representation of neonates in antibiotic clinical trials, are key issues impeding optimal treatment. Research and programmatic interventions to accelerate neonatal sepsis prevention and treatment should be prioritized alongside preterm birth prevention. Key actions include improving clinical care and infection prevention practices, and developing new diagnostic tests and vaccines that target the most common neonatal sepsis pathogens, particularly those responsible for the greatest morbidity and mortality.

title: Beyond the worm: engineering the next generation of nematode-inspired antimicrobials
abstract: The global crisis of multidrug-resistant bacteria and parasitic nematodes demands new approaches to infectious disease control. Emerging evidence suggests that gastrointestinal nematodes and the host gut microbiota are inextricably linked in a complex 'holobiont'. Parasitic nematodes have evolved in microbe-rich environments for millennia, developing innate immune defenses. This evolutionary 'arms race' has produced a diverse repertoire of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) that can target bacteria and other gut microbiota. With over 5000 AMP and AMP-like domain-encoding genes identified via computational mining, the bottleneck is validation. The integration of machine learning algorithms with advanced in vitro and ex vivo models will allow prediction of AMP mode of action, spectrum of activity, and efficacy, followed by testing in organoids to address some of the limitations of animal models.

title: Helicobacter pylori antibiotic resistance in Egypt exceeds eradication thresholds: systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Eradicating Helicobacter pylori in Egypt is severely hindered by escalating antibiotic resistance. Comprehensive national resistance data are essential for optimizing failing treatment protocols. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the pooled prevalence of Helicobacter pylori resistance to key antibiotics in Egypt to inform national treatment guidelines. Data sources: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Egyptian Knowledge Bank (EKB). Primary studies published between 2000 and 2025 reporting H. pylori antibiotic resistance prevalence in Egypt were included. Human subjects with documented H. pylori infection. Resistance was assessed for metronidazole, amoxicillin, clarithromycin, tetracycline, and fluoroquinolones. Assessment of risk of bias: The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prevalence Studies was used. Methods of data synthesis: Pooled prevalence and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a random-effects model with Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation. Thirty studies comprising 5019 observations were included. The resistance rate for clarithromycin was 42.8% (95% CI: 34.7-51.1%), nearly tripling the 15% Maastricht clinical threshold for abandoning empirical clarithromycin-containing regimens. Rates for other primary antibiotics were also critically high: metronidazole 79.1% (95% CI: 64.7-90.8%) and amoxicillin 45.8% (95% CI: 29.1-62.9%), both far exceeding rates typical for standard empirical therapies. Resistance to tetracycline (23.4%), ciprofloxacin (20.0%), and levofloxacin (18.8%) also surpassed clinical cutoffs. Significant geographic disparities were observed across governorates, with metronidazole resistance reaching 100% in some regions. Meta-regression indicated that these high resistance levels have remained stable over the past two decades. Egypt Delta and the Cairo metropolitan areas face a critical burden of Helicobacter pylori resistance, rendering standard empirical triple therapies suboptimal. National guidelines should prioritise quadruple therapy or susceptibility-guided treatments to improve eradication outcomes. PROSPERO (CRD420251249967).

title: Streptococcus thoraltensis in a Postoperative Wound Infection and a Therapeutic Regimen Associated with Successful Eradication
abstract: is commonly isolated from swine and rabbits; however, over the past decade, it has caused various infections in human beings. The treatment of these infections is typically complex because of an association with antibiotic resistance. A 20-year-old female patient presented with a postoperative surgical site infection and a positive culture for, representing a clinical combination not previously described. A favorable response was achieved by implementing a treatment regimen based on surgical wound cleansing with an isotonic and stabilized 0.057% sodium hypochlorite antimicrobial solution, followed by the application of a gel of the same composition, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, and the use of a Negative Pressure Wound Therapy. The relevance of this case lies in its presentation of a new clinical manifestation of the infection, marking the third report and fifth case described within the Mexican population. Above all, it outlines a therapeutic protocol that achieved favorable outcomes, providing a valuable reference for future cases.

title: Genomic profiling of maternal Streptococcus agalactiae reveals prophage-associated resistance and comparative characterization of anovaginal and respiratory isolates
authors: de Abreu Pereira MDC et al.
abstract: Maternal colonization with Streptococcus agalactiae (GBS) is a major risk factor for neonatal diseases. While anovaginal screening is the primary guide for antibiotic prophylaxis, the upper respiratory tract is an understudied potential reservoir for GBS disease. However, the maternal carriage, serotype distribution, and genetic determinants of respiratory colonization remain unknown. To investigate the prevalence and genomic determinants of antimicrobial resistance and virulence in anovaginal and nasal GBS carriage among pregnant women using molecular methods and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Paired nasal and anovaginal swabs were collected from 221 pregnant women. Colonization and capsular serotypes were detected using cfb- and cps-targeted qPCR, along with standard culture. Subsequently, the recovered isolates were subjected to antimicrobial susceptibility testing and WGS for pan-genomic and phylogenomic analyses. The overall GBS colonization prevalence was 24%, comprising 22.6% anovaginal and 2.3% nasal carriers. Notably, 49% of the positive samples were detected exclusively by qPCR, which also revealed multi-serotype co-colonization in 7.5% of the colonized women. Serotypes Ia and V were the most prevalent. Erythromycin resistance reached 31%, largely associated with a prophage harboring mefA-msrD within Tn1207.1. WGS revealed CC23 as the major lineage, which clustered with the nasal isolates. Furthermore, an exploratory hypothesis-generating pangenome analysis, suggested a potential association between respiratory isolates and a prophage encoding stress-response gene. Molecular screening outperformed standard culture, revealing hidden epidemiological complexities, including underreported co-colonization. The high prevalence of macrolide resistance associated with prophage-borne genes highlights the need for continuous genomic surveillance to track potentially emerging GBS lineages in maternal care.

title: State of the Art of Treatment of Acinetobacter baumannii Infections
abstract: complex is the most commonly identified group of species within the genusand has globally emerged as a major health care-associated pathogen.is the species most frequently responsible for human infections and has been classified by the World Health Organization as a critical-priority pathogen because of its remarkable ability to acquire antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and the high attributable mortality associated with its infections, which can reach 70% in critically ill patients. This section reviews the global and regional epidemiology of, its complex mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance, and current therapeutic strategies, with particular emphasis on newly approved antimicrobial agents.

title: Comparative Analysis of Phenotypic Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance Among Aeromonas veronii Strains Isolated from Different Farmed Freshwater Fish
abstract: is an important zoonotic pathogen causing severe diseases and high mortality in freshwater aquaculture. In this study, five strains (LY-3, JY-1, G7, G8, and WL-3) were isolated from different diseased freshwater fish in Linyi City, Shandong Province, China, and identified asusing phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA andB sequences. Five strains grew at 20-40°C, pH 5.0-8.0, and 0-3% NaCl, demonstrating strong environmental tolerance. Their optimal temperature and pH were identical, but optimal NaCl concentration was strain-dependent. Despite harboring the hemolysin-related genes,, and, all strains except JY-1 exhibited β-hemolytic activity. All strains exhibited distinct flagella-driven motility abilities. Specifically, only strain G8 possessed two polar flagella and exhibited the strongest swimming motility. Similarly, all strains formed biofilms, correlating with the production of N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL). Worryingly, all strains exhibited multi-drug resistance to three penicillin-class antibiotics, midecamycin, clindamycin, three carbapenems, vancomycin, and polymyxin B. Additionally, five strains carriedandgenes, and four strains (excluding LY-3) additionally harbored thegene. Encouragingly, most of isolates remained susceptible to florfenicol and enrofloxacin. These results indicate considerable intra-specific heterogeneity amongstrains from different geographical origins and host sources, suggesting an urgent need for precise treatments.

title: Exploring the potential of herbal nanotechnology for the treatment of urinary tract infections
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) continue to pose a substantial clinical challenge due to high recurrence, biofilm-mediated persistence, and the rapid expansion of antimicrobial resistance. The waning effectiveness of conventional antibiotics highlights the urgency for resistance-sparing therapeutic strategies. Recent advances in herbal nanotechnology have enabled the precise nanoengineering of plant-derived phytochemicals, enhancing their stability, bioavailability, and pathogen-specific activity. This review critically appraises nanomaterial-based phytotherapeutic approaches for UTI management, focusing on the mechanistic integration of phytochemical bioactivity with nanoscale delivery systems. Nanomaterials developed from medicinal plants, crude extracts, and isolated phytoconstituents are evaluated for their ability to interfere with uropathogen adhesion, dismantle biofilms, suppress virulence signaling, induce oxidative stress, and regulate host inflammatory responses. Translational barriers, including formulation reproducibility, safety assessment, scalable production, and regulatory compliance, are also examined. By consolidating antimicrobial, antibiofilm, and host-modulatory evidence, this review identifies nano-enabled phytotherapeutic strategies with translational promise as multi-target alternatives to antibiotic-based UTI therapy.

title: One health molecular epidemiology of carbapenem- and colistin-resistant Escherichia coli sequence types in humans, poultry, and the environment in Pakistan
abstract: The emergence of antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is a grave One Health concern, leading to increased mortality and economic loss globally. These pathogens have acquired several resistance genes against WHO-defined medically important classes of antibiotics. Therefore, we plan to investigate AMR prevalence within the One Health framework. A total of 300 samples (100 each from human clinical, poultry, and environmental sources) were collected aseptically. We cultured isolates using standard microbiological methods and identified them with the VITEK2 Compact system. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed according to CLSI guidelines. Two-locus CH typing was used to assign sequence types (STs), and PCR was performed to detect bla, bla, bla, bla, and mcr-1. A total of 27 carbapenem-resistant E. coli (CR-EC) and 3 colistin-resistant E. coli (ColR-EC) isolates were recovered from human samples, 38 CR-EC and 5 ColR-EC from environmental samples, and 25 ColR-EC from poultry samples. Among all isolates, ST101 (21/90; 23.3%), ST131 (15/90; 16.7%), and ST405 (15/90; 16.7%) were the predominant sequence types. All three reservoirs harboured ST101, ST131, and ST405, while ST648 was shared between human and environmental isolates, and ST10 was shared between poultry and environmental isolates. Among environmental carbapenem-resistant isolates, bla(20/38; 52.6%), bla(18/38; 47.4%), bla(11/38; 28.9%), bla(6/38; 15.8%), and mcr-1 (5/38; 13.2%) were detected. All human carbapenem-resistant isolates carried bla(27/27; 100%), whereas all poultry colistin-resistant isolates harboured mcr-1 (25/25; 100%). High-risk multidrug-resistant E. coli lineages carrying carbapenemase and colistin resistance genes are widely distributed across human, poultry, and environmental reservoirs, highlighting the interconnected nature of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Molecular characterization of virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance determinants in Arcobacter butzleri isolated from seafood of the Mumbai coast, India
abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the occurrence of Arcobacter butzleri in seafood from the Mumbai coast, India and evaluated its genetic potential associated with virulence and antimicrobial resistance through comprehensive analysis of virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. Among the 70 samples screened, 44 were positive for A. butzleri, resulting in an overall prevalence of 62.86%. A higher rate of prevalence was reported from bivalves (84.62%), followed by crustaceans (78.57%), finfish (60.61%) and cephalopods (33.33%). Characterization of isolates based on putative virulence-associated genes revealed that most of them harboured more than five genes. Genes such as tlyA, cadF, ciaB, mviN and pldA were found dominant, whereas irgA and hecA were the limiting ones. Sample level characterization of total number of virulence-associated genes yielded significant differences among the seafood categories tested, with significant association between iroE gene and the sample category (P < 0.05). Phenotypic analysis of antibiotic susceptibility revealed 88.1% of the isolates to be multidrug resistant, with an average MAR indices of 0.39. The β-lactam resistant gene (bla) was found to be the dominant gene in the present study, followed by macA. This study, underscores the significance of seafood as a possible carrier of pathogenic and antimicrobial-resistant A. butzleri and emphasizes the need for continuous surveillance and implementation of stringent hygienic practices.

title: De Novo Design of Multi-Mechanistic AIE Photosensitizer for Broad-Spectrum Bacterial Eradication
abstract: Antibiotic resistance poses a serious threat to human health. Inspired by the clinical practice of employing drug combinations to achieve combined effects, we hypothesized that integrating multiple mechanisms into a single molecule could address drug-resistant bacterial infections. Based on a propeller-modification strategy and dual alkyl-chain engineering, we de novo designed and synthesized a C2-symmetric propeller-shaped aggregation-induced emission photosensitizer. After iterative screening, the optimized compound MeOTDP-2 exhibits broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, enabling efficient eradication of planktonic bacteria, drug-resistant strains, polymicrobial infections, biofilms, and persister cells, with no cellular invasiveness and negligible cytotoxicity. Mechanistic studies revealed that MeOTDP-2 achieves chemo-photodynamic combined antibacterial therapy by targeting and disrupting bacterial membranes and DNA, alongside light-mediated intracellular reactive oxygen species accumulation. Furthermore, in mouse models of MRSA-induced skin abscess and full-thickness skin wound infection, MeOTDP-2 demonstrated superior therapeutic efficacy to vancomycin. This strategy, integrating dual targeting with multiple mechanisms, offers new promise for overcoming bacterial resistance.

title: Nucleic Acid Aptamers in Bacteriology: Mapping the Landscape, Exploring Bioimaging Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is becoming increasingly widespread, underlining the importance of rapid, accurate identification of bacterial infections for effective diagnostic, clinical, and environmental management. While next-generation sequencing excels at genetic characterization, it falls short in real-time, in situ detection, a critical gap where nucleic acid aptamers emerge as a compelling alternative. These synthetic oligonucleotides enable direct, low-cost, and versatile detection of bacterial targets without requiring DNA extraction or amplification. Their portability supports point-of-care diagnostics, while their molecular precision enables integration into advanced bioimaging platforms for non-invasive, real-time, spatial, and functional monitoring of pathogens in biological environments. This perspective explores the potential of aptamers for bacterial bioimaging, assessing the landscape of bacterial-targeting aptamers, zooming in on aptamer-based bioimaging approaches for bacterial detection, addressing key challenges, and outlining future opportunities, such as real-time dynamic infection imaging and theranostics, polyclonal/multivalent aptamers, multiplex imaging, aptamer-based biosensors, and AI-driven detection.

title: Spatiotemporal recurrence and dissemination of Salmonella subpopulations in surface waters of central Chile
abstract: Agricultural waters have been identified as one of the primary sources ofcontamination, which has resulted in numerous outbreaks associated with the consumption of contaminated produce. Consequently, an improved understanding ofcontamination of agricultural waters could facilitate the development of control strategies to prevent food contamination. The objective of this study was to examine the diversity and spatiotemporal recurrence ofisolates in surface water related to agricultural activities. Water samples (= 2,690) were collected between 2019 and 2024 in central Chile using modified Moore swabs, and whole-genome sequencing was carried out for 1 to 10isolates per sample. Non-clonal genomes from each sample (= 1,034) were analyzed, showing that the most frequently identified serovars were Infantis (14.6%), Typhimurium (10.8%), Newport (8.5%), and Enteritidis (5.8%). The highest antimicrobial resistance burden was shown byInfantis, which carried up to 11 antimicrobial resistance genes simultaneously. Importantly, phylogenomic analyses revealed a highly clonal population structure among the most prevalent serovars and identified recurrent subpopulations that were repeatedly detected across multiple watersheds and consecutive years, including lineages associated with human infections. These findings provide genomic evidence that agricultural surface waters may serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrentsubpopulations in central Chile, including multidrug-resistant strains. Our work underscores the critical importance of continuous environmental surveillance and the integration of environmental and clinical genomic surveillance data to improve our understanding of theecology and inform evidence-based mitigation strategies aiming to protect public health.IMPORTANCEis a leading cause of foodborne illness worldwide, and contaminated irrigation water is an important pathway by which this pathogen can reach fresh produce. By analyzing more than 1,000genomes collected from agricultural waters in central Chile over 5 years, we found that specific bacterial lineages persisted across multiple watersheds and years, including multidrug-resistant strains linked to human infections. These findings indicate that agricultural surface waters in Chile can serve as reservoirs and dissemination routes for recurrentsubpopulations. Our study highlights the value of continuous environmental surveillance and the need to integrate data from environmental and human sources to identify potential contamination sources and reduce the risk of foodborne disease.

title: Dynamics of within-host genomic relatedness and emergence of resistance in serial Mycobacterium avium complex isolates during treatment
abstract: complex infections require prolonged multidrug therapy and may develop antimicrobial resistance. We applied whole-genome sequencing (WGS) to assess within-patient genomic relatedness and resistance-associated mutations emerging during therapy. WGS was performed on cultured populations of 30 serial isolates (16and 14) from 13 patients with repeated recovery of the same species. Genomic relatedness was classified by species/subspecies, sequence type (ST), and fastBAPS (FB) clustering. Resistance-associated mutations were assessed in isolates showing susceptible-to-resistant conversion or an increase of at least two dilutions in the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Among 13 patients, 10 (76.9%) showed concordant genomic patterns, 2 (15.4%) showed discordant genomic patterns with genetically distinct cultured populations, and 1 (7.7%) showed both concordant and discordant relationships across intervals. Sixteencultured populations belonged to four STs (ST112 and ST118, 75.0%) and four FB clusters. Fourteencultured populations belonged to four STs, predominantly ST1109 (71.4%). While most cultured populations of the same ST matched the same FB,ST112 and ST118 andST1109 each occurred in two FB clusters. Conversely, three STs (ST112, ST118, and ST1112) ofbelonged to the same FB. Among three cases with emergent clarithromycin resistance,mutations (A2058C and A2059G) were identified in two. In one case, anintergenic variant showed stepwise increases in variant allele frequency, accompanied by increasing ethambutol MICs. WGS provided two methods for analyzing within-patient genomic relatedness (ST assignment and FB clustering), which were mutually complementary and enabled longitudinal detection of resistance-associated mutations during treatment. complex pulmonary disease often requires prolonged multidrug therapy, during which serial culture-positive isolates may differ in within-patient genomic relatedness and antimicrobial resistance. Distinguishing closely related from genetically distinct isolates and identifying emerging resistance are clinically important but cannot be reliably achieved using conventional species identification or sequence typing alone. In this study, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of serialcomplex isolates enabled high-resolution assessment of within-patient genomic relatedness. WGS also identified emerging resistance-associated mutations, including acquiredmutations associated with high-level clarithromycin resistance during macrolide-containing therapy and anintergenic variant accompanying increasing ethambutol minimum inhibitory concentrations during ethambutol-containing treatment. These findings support the potential clinical utility of WGS for characterizing genomic relationships among recurrentcomplex isolates and detecting emergence of resistance-associated mutations during therapy.

title: Draft genome sequence of Enterococcus faecalis strain MBBL_RBS1 isolated from a dairy cow with repeat breeding syndrome
abstract: We report the draft genome ofstrain MBBL_RBS1, isolated from uterine discharge of a repeat-breeder dairy cow in Bangladesh. The 2.740 Mbp genome comprises 25 contigs, with 37.5% GC content, 6 antimicrobial resistance genes, 24 virulence genes, and a PathogenFinder-predicted probability of human pathogenicity of 0.889.

title: Pathogen identification and resistance gene expression tests using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension in gram-negative contrived positive blood cultures
abstract: Rapid pathogen identification, resistance detection, and susceptibility profiling improve antimicrobial prescribing and associated outcomes, but fragmented workflows lead to inefficiencies and are costly. We evaluated a research-use-only (RUO) approach using ASTar remnant bacterial suspension from routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) for matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) pathogen identification and lateral flow assay (LFA)-based detection of targeted resistance mechanisms. Gram-negative bacterial strains from reference and curated resistance collections (CDC1, ARLG2, and ATCC3) (= 129) were contrived into blood culture bottles and processed in the ASTar System using the ASTar BC G- Kit (Q-linea AB, Sweden). Under RUO conditions, remnant bacterial suspensions were collected ~1-2 h after ASTar run initiation and analyzed using NG Test CTX-M Multi, NG Test CARBA-5, NG Test Acineto-5 RUO, and MALDI-TOF MS. Mean (±SD) remnant suspension volume was 2,722 μL (±300 µL). All samples yielded high-confidence MALDI-TOF MS scores (>2.0), with five initially scoring <2.0 and resolving on repeat testing. LFA results showed full agreement with reference isolates forpositive/negative (32/32) and with 60 or 61 target carbapenemase-positive/negative isolates. Testing of a subset of samples to mimic reflex workflows with ASTar phenotypic results did not affect LFA performance (= 35; 23 Enterobacterales, 3, and 9). Cost savings can be realized versus commercial multiplex PCR. This integrated approach of ~6 h rapid phenotypic AST with same-run identification and resistance detection (1-2 h from instrument start) or reflex testing upon availability of ASTar results may support earlier susceptibility results and offer cost savings to current workflows.IMPORTANCERapid, integrated diagnostic workflows are recommended and essential for improving patient outcomes in bloodstream infections, where delays in pathogen identification and resistance detection can compromise timely antimicrobial therapy. Current workflows often rely on multiple platforms, increasing turnaround time and laboratory burden. Additionally, the clinical impact of rapid diagnostic results is dependent on timely interpretation and implementation within antimicrobial stewardship frameworks, which may involve complex decision algorithms. This study demonstrates that remnant bacterial suspensions generated during routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) using the ASTar System can be recovered and utilized for rapid matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry and lateral flow assay-based resistance detection. By enabling pathogen identification and/or resistance detection within ~1-2 h of AST initiation or resistance detection via reflex testing, this approach reduces duplicate sample testing and may enable earlier access to rapid microbiological results.

Optimal One Health control of antimicrobial resistance: a household mean-field model with community feedback and parameters from Burkina Faso
abstract: We study how to combine three One Health interventions against antimicrobial resistance: prescription-only dispensing of antibiotics to people, access to veterinary care for animals, and treatment of household sludge and manure. Each household is a Markov chain on the carriage states of its people, animals and soil, and households are linked through the community, whose prevalence feeds the acquisition rates. We prove that, as the number of households grows, the distribution of household states converges to the solution of a nonlinear mean-field equation. This system is monotone for the stochastic order, so that no intervention increases carriage anywhere, and for every constant intervention it has exactly one equilibrium, which attracts all solutions and is given by a scalar equation. For the optimal control problem we prove existence, necessary conditions, positivity of all controls under a quadratic cost, uniqueness for short horizons, and a turnpike property under an explicit dissipativity condition, which we verify for our parameters by a computer-assisted numerical certification. With parameters from Tenkodogo, Burkina Faso, the optimal combined strategy averts about 17% of human carriage over three years in the baseline scenario, and 11% to 28% over the plausible scenarios for the parameters that the survey cannot identify; these figures are projections conditional on the model. The strategy itself is robust: the value of perfect information on the unmeasured parameters is about 2% of the achievable benefit. A compartmental model with the same transmission rates but without households underestimates the benefit, and targeting the interventions by zone of the town increases it.

title: Innovative Approaches in the Treatment of Acne Vulgaris: A Comprehensive Review of Current and Emerging Therapies
abstract: The prevalence rates of acne vulgaris, a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder that mostly affects adolescents and young adults, range from 35% to over 90%. It can significantly impair quality of life and contribute to physical and psychological distress. Chemical peels, photodynamic therapy, and topical pharmaceutical combinations have been found to be successful treatments for mild-to-moderate acne. This study examines the many approaches being used to treat acne vulgaris. These include both established treatments like topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin, as well as newer approaches including phototherapy, biologics, and innovative combination therapies. This review's goals are to assess the efficacy of current therapies, investigate cutting-edge methods for treating acne, and offer suggestions for future lines of inquiry and clinical application. The results highlight the value of individualized treatment plans and the necessity of continued study to address issues like patient adherence and antibiotic resistance. Notwithstanding these developments, further research is desperately needed to develop novel treatments that can improve patient outcomes even more. This is especially true when it comes to addressing treatment resistance and customizing care plans to maximize effectiveness and reduce adverse effects. More research into personalized medicine techniques could result in more specialized and efficient acne vulgaris treatment solutions.

title: Vaginal and uterine volatile organic compound profiles, bacterial isolates, and antimicrobial susceptibility in canine pyometra
abstract: Canine pyometra is a life-threatening uterine disease requiring timely diagnosis and appropriate antimicrobial treatment. This study characterized uterine bacteria and antimicrobial susceptibility and compared vaginal and uterine volatile organic compound (VOC) profiles in 27 bitches with pyometra (14 open-cervix, 13 closed-cervix) and 14 healthy controls. Uterine isolates were identified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and susceptibility was assessed by disk diffusion. Vaginal and uterine swabs were analyzed by headspace solid-phase microextraction-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Aerobic bacterial growth occurred in 17/27 pyometra cases (63.0%), yielding nine species; Escherichia coli was most frequent (4/17 isolates; 23.5%). Chloramphenicol had the highest proportion of susceptible isolates (94.1%), whereas cephalexin had the highest resistance proportion (58.8%); one E. coli isolate was multidrug resistant. Among eight shared VOC features, VOC-1 and VOC-2 had greater peak areas in vaginal (P = 0.004 and 0.005) and uterine (P = 0.002 and 0.001) pyometra samples than controls. VOC-3 differed significantly only in uterine samples (P = 0.009). However, vaginal VOC-1, VOC-2, and VOC-3 did not significantly distinguish closed-cervix pyometra from healthy controls. Compound assignments were tentative (Metabolomics Standards Initiative Level 2/3), based on library matches without confirmation using authentic standards. These exploratory findings characterize uterine bacterial isolates, antimicrobial susceptibility, and vaginal and uterine VOC profiles in canine pyometra. Chemical confirmation and validation in larger independent cohorts are required before diagnostic application, particularly in closed-cervix cases.

Electrocatalytic ozonation for removal of pharmaceuticals, pathogenic microorganisms, and antibiotic resistance genes from hospital wastewater
abstract: The widespread use of antibiotics, particularly in hospital wastewater, accelerates the proliferation of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs), posing a global threat. To address this challenge, an efficient electrocatalytic ozonation (ECO) process was constructed by injecting diffused ozone bubbles, using stainless steel and graphite as the anode and cathode. The ECO system exhibited superior catalytic performance in degrading dexamethasone (DXMS) with pseudo-first-order reaction rate constants (k, 0.401 min), which is 4 and 93 times higher than those of ozonation and electrolysis alone, respectively. Hydroxyl radicals(OH) were identified as the primary reactive species. The ECO process effectively reduced bacterial culturability of Escherichia coli (E. coli) in 5 min by disrupting cell integrity and DNA structure. In real hospital wastewater treatment, the ECO system maintained a COD removal efficiency of 72.25% - 86.82% and eliminated 81 of the 119 detected pharmaceutical contaminants, achieving an average removal rate of 85.42%. The removal efficiencies for various ARGs ranged from -7.73-99.13%. The ECO process effectively caused substantial DNA degradation and altered the relative abundance of ARGs and microbial taxa in hospital wastewater. Collectively, these results demonstrate that the ECO system holds significant potential for the simultaneous removal of pharmaceuticals, pathogens, and ARGs from hospital wastewater.

title: Targeted Protein Degradation as a Novel Drug Discovery Platform for Antimicrobial Resistance: PROTACs, BacPROTACs, and Beyond
abstract: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) represents one of the growing global public health concerns, demanding the development of novel therapeutic modalities based on mechanisms of action different from those of conventional occupancy-based inhibitors. Targeted Protein Degradation (TPD), specifically Proteolysis- targeting Chimeras (PROTACs), provides a new concept in which bacterial proteins can be degraded rather than temporarily inhibited. In this review, we discuss the development of PROTAC technology and its potential in the field of antibacterial drug discovery. The FDA Approval of Vepdegestrant (ARV-471), the first clinically approved TPD drug, in May 2026 represents a milestone in this area. Among the approaches used for antibacterial purposes, BacPROTACs and Homo-BacPROTACs, which aim to degrade proteins in the Clp protease network in bacteria, represent strong examples of this concept and have demonstrated selective protein degradation, antibiotic resensitization, and bactericidal activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains, including drug-resistant ones. These findings provide strong evidence for the feasibility of using the bacterial proteostasis network for the development of an antibacterial treatment based on protein degradation. Nevertheless, clinical translation still faces challenges due to large molecular size, poor solubility, limited permeability, kinetic limitations, cellular delivery, bacterial efflux, and limited applicability to Gramnegative pathogens. Continued innovation is needed to make antibacterial TPD clinically viable.

title: Unveiling the Antimicrobial Potential of Syzygium cumini: Medicinal Benefits, Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives
abstract: The traditional system of medicine has used the medicinal plant Syzygium cumini, also referred to as jamun. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance has prompted exploration of the natural constituents of Syzygium cumini as a potential source for bioactive compounds. The plant contains diverse phytochemicals, including flavonoids (quercetin, myricetin), phenolic acids (ellagic acid, gallic acid), tannins, alkaloids, and anthocyanins, which exhibit antibacterial and antifungal activity. Review studies show that the plant has a broad spectrum of antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral properties through various mechanisms, including membrane damage and inhibition of enzymatic activity. Naturally, advancements have improved the bioavailability and stability of phytochemicals in the contents of Syzygium cumini. Challenges such as the absence of standardisation, the need to refine isolation methods, and the need for clinical validation despite promising results in vitro and in vivo have also been observed. This review discusses recent advancements and potential areas for future exploration in the development of antimicrobial agents.

title: Rapid Point-of-Care Quantification of Urinary Tract Infection Biomarker Xanthine Oxidase
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a growing global health threat. Overuse of antimicrobial drugs is a main driver of resistance, with urinary tract infections (UTIs) a common indication for antibiotic use. To improve UTI treatment and reduce antimicrobial resistance, real-time diagnostic tools for monitoring the host immune response are needed. Xanthine oxidase (XO) is an enzyme that is elevated in UTIs and shows potential for sensitive and selective detection of infection. We developed a rapid and sensitive point-of-care electrochemical sensor for XO detection by using a simple manufacturing approach. The sensor consists of a disposable carbon electrode embedded in a capillary fill chamber designed for point-of-care sample collection. After urine collection, XO catalyzes its substrate while changing the oxidation state of a secondary electron acceptor. The magnitude and rate of this redox shift reflects XO activity, enabling quantification of XO in urine. We demonstrate minimal intersensor variability of less than 5%, resulting in a calibration with anof 0.985 across eight individual sensors. The capillary fill device was optimized to enable efficient substrate dissolution, reducing the time to result from 10 min to just 2 min. This approach enables calibration-free detection of XO in artificial and spiked human urine samples within 2 min of sample collection in both artificial urine and spiked human urine samples.

title: Unveiling novel therapeutic targets and potent hits to combat antimicrobial resistance in Bacteroides fragilis
abstract: The opportunistic anaerobic bacterium Bacteroides fragilis is an important human pathogen associated with a variety of infections, including intra-abdominal abscesses, peritonitis, bacteremia, lung abscesses and surgical site infections. The growing number of strains that are multidrug-resistant (MDR) in B. fragilis has raised attention to identify new therapeutic targets and discover potent antimicrobial drugs. An integrative computational approach was used in this study to highlight promising inhibitors against B. fragilis and identify potential therapeutic targets. The present study identified 18 essential proteins from the B. fragilis proteome that contribute to virulence and pathogenicity and play critical roles in bacterial survival. Furthermore, protein-protein interactions (PPI's) network analysis, functional annotation, and enrichment analyses identified tetraacyldisaccharide 4'-kinase (LpxK) as the most promising druggable target, owing to its essential role in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis in Gram-negative bacteria. Structure-guided drug design identified five high-affinity LpxK inhibitors. DFT and molecular dynamics analyses confirmed stable binding and conformational stability. Furthermore, these findings provide a theoretical basis for the rational development of targeted antibacterial agents against multidrug-resistant B. fragilis towards infectious disease control, and lay the foundation for future experimental evaluation and optimization.
